newsitem.title: CANADA: ICE HOCKEY-MOUNTIES ARREST CANADIAN HOCKEY DEAL MAKER ON FRAUD.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-MOUNTIES ARREST CANADIAN HOCKEY DEAL MAKER ON FRAUD.

text.p: Ice hockey deal-maker Alan
Eagleson, who faces a bevy of charges in the United States,
was arrested on eight counts of fraud and theft Tuesday after
a three-year investigation, police said.
Eagleson turned himself in to police in a community just
outside of Toronto and will appear in court on December 16,
according to a statement from the Royal Canadian Mounted
Police.
Eagleson's longtime business associate, Arthur Harnett,
was charged with four counts of fraud and theft.
Eagleson, the former Executive Director of the National
Hockey League Players' Association and a director of Hockey
Canada, has been under suspicion here and in the United States
on the handling of funds from international tournaments and in
his actions as an agent for professional hockey players.
Canadian police have travelled to Europe and the United
States to investigate advertising revenue from the now defunct
international event called the Canada Cup, precursor to the
World Cup. Mortgage funds from the NHL Players' Association
were also being traced, police said.
Eagleson was a household name in Canada for his
high-profile deal making in Canada's national sport. He
organised an historic matchup between Canada's professionals
and the Soviet Union's best in 1972 and then went on to
organise five Canada Cup tournaments that included national
teams from all the hockey powers.
Eagleson also faces problems in the United States. A
Boston grand jury indicted him on 32 charges of fraud,
racketeering and embezzlement and an extradition application
for him is before the U.S. Justice Department.
As well, some former NHL players have filed a class-action
suit against him in Philadelphia.
The charges against Harnett and Eagleson concern more than
$200,000 (US $148,000) in payments by Eagleson on behalf of
Hockey Canada to companies owned by Harnett.
Eagleson alone faces charges relating to the sale of
advertising on the sides of hockey rink boards during the
Canada Cup tournaments.
The NHL Players' Association said Tuesday it was now hoping
that an end could be brought to an "unfortunate" period in
professional hockey.
"Only by having all legal proceedings brought to a final
conclusion can this unfortunate part of our past be resolved
once and for all," said Bob Goodenow, the NHLPA's Executive
Director and General Counsel, in a statement.
